summary: Revolutionary soldier who escaped from a British island prison and became a Plymouth militia colonel; husband of John's 5th-great-grand-aunt Elizabeth Lamoreaux.
bio:
George Palmer Ransom was born at Canaan, Litchfield Co., CT, in 1762, or in 1761 according to his neighbour of twenty years, the historian H. B. Wright. His father, Captain Samuel Ransom, was killed at the Battle of Wyoming in 1778; his remains were later found "with the head severed from the body". George served as orderly-sergeant in his father's company at Millstone, Bound Brook, Germantown and Brandywine. On 6 December 1780 he had gone "a sparking" in his best regimentals to old Benjamin Harvey's log house at Plymouth when six Indians burst in and carried off the household. He was imprisoned on Prisoners' Island in the St. Lawrence River, and in 1782 swam the river and escaped through the woods to Vermont.

Back in Plymouth, Luzerne County, Pennsylvania, he commanded the local militia company as captain in 1790, when Thomas Lamoreaux served under him, and rose to colonel. In 1794 he married Elizabeth Lamoreaux, John's 5th-great-grand-aunt. A county history tells how he was fined one cent by the Luzerne court for knocking down a man who had insulted Washington. He farmed and built a sawmill in 1815 in what became Jackson Township, which his son Chester replaced in 1840. One daughter married the schoolmaster Charles C. Curtis and inherited the Jackson Township farm; another, Livia, married Oliver Davenport.

He lived and died in the "old red mansion house" on the Plymouth flats, where the town pound stood on his land. In 1845 he was 82 and lame, and his grandson George Palmer Steele had just finished a term as sheriff of Luzerne. Wright's history of Plymouth carries his portrait, "taken at 85". He died in 1850.

events.title: Revolutionary service in his father's company
events.description: Orderly-sergeant in Capt. Samuel Ransom's Independent Company; 'gained some credit for his valor at Millstone, Boundbrook, Germantown and Brandywine'. [R4-S1]

events.title: Captured by Indians
events.description: He had put on his best regimentals to go courting at old Benjamin Harvey's. Six Indians took the elder Harvey, his son Elisha, Lois (Louisa) Harvey, Lucy Bullford and Ransom; the women were released on Shawnee Mountain. [R4-S1]

events.title: Imprisoned and escaped
events.description: Moved from Montreal to Prisoner's Island in Feb 1781; swam the St. Lawrence and, with two others, made his way through the forest to Vermont and then Connecticut. His account was taken down by Charles Miner as part of 'The Hazleton Travellers'. [R4-S1] [R4-S3]

events.title: Fined one cent for defending Washington's name
events.place: Luzerne County Court of Quarter Sessions, Wilkes-Barre
events.description: Pleaded guilty to knocking down a young man who had abused the name of General Washington. Judge Scott left the case to his associate judges (old soldiers Hollenback and Fell), who fined Ransom one cent and made the prosecutor pay costs. [R4-S2]

events.title: Built a sawmill
events.description: Torn down in 1840 and replaced by his son Chester. [R4-S3]

researchNotes:
Col. George Palmer Ransom (1762-1850) married Elizabeth Lamoreaux in 1794. His father, Capt. Samuel Ransom, was killed in the 1778 Battle of Wyoming, his remains later found 'with the head severed from the body'. George was captured in 1780 and escaped from Prisoners' Island in the St. Lawrence River in 1782. In October 1790 Thomas Lamoreaux served in Capt. George P. Ransom's militia company at Plymouth.

Col. H. B. Wright lived next door to Colonel Ransom for twenty years. In his Historical Sketches of Plymouth (1873) he says Ransom was born at Canaan, Litchfield Co., Conn., in 1761. He served as orderly-sergeant in his father's company at Millstone, Bound Brook, Germantown and Brandywine. On 6 Dec 1780 he had gone 'a sparking' in his best regimentals to old Benjamin Harvey's house when six Indians burst in and carried off the household. After imprisonment on Prisoner's Island in the St. Lawrence he swam the river and escaped through the woods to Vermont. He lived and died in the 'old red mansion house' on the Plymouth flats, and the town pound stood on his land. Wright's book has his portrait 'taken at 85' ([R4-S1]). Charles Miner noted in 1845 that he was 82 and lame, and that his grandson George Palmer Steele had just finished a term as sheriff of Luzerne ([R4-S3]). A later county history tells how he was fined one cent for knocking down a man who had insulted Washington ([R4-S2]). He built a sawmill in 1815, and his son Chester replaced it in 1840 ([R4-S3]). One daughter married the schoolmaster Charles C. Curtis and inherited the Jackson Twp. farm ([R4-S1]). Another, Livia, married Oliver Davenport (Bradsby).
